study_data.study_comment: The study is about investigating whether changes in the Simon effect can be explained solely by the temporal fading of irrelevant response activation or whether additional cognitive mechanisms contribute to these effects. To examine this, the authors combined delta plot analyses with experimental manipulations targeting different processing stages: perceptual processing (stimulus discriminability), decision processes (number of response alternatives and stimulus- response associations), and motor execution (hand vs. foot responses)—within a visual Simon task.

publication_data.title: Beyond mean reaction times: Combining distributional analyses with processing stage manipulations in the Simon task
publication_data.apa_reference: Mittelstädt, V., & Miller, J. (2020). Beyond mean reaction times: Combining distributional analyses with processing stage manipulations in the Simon task. Cognitive Psychology, 119, 101275. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2020.101275
publication_data.keywords: Simon effect, delta plots, information processing, task performance, reaction time

task_data.task_description: Participants are required to make a key press response to the color of a stimulus presented on the left or right side of a fixation cross. For each participant, two stimulus colors were selected randomly from a set of four colors (red, blue, green, yellow), with one each assigned to the left and right hand. To manipulate the duration of perceptual processes stimulus discriminability was varied between blocks. Stimulus discriminability was manipulated by varying the thickness and the color saturation (RGB values) of the lines of the squares.

Participants are required to make a key press response to the color of a stimulus presented on the left or right side of a fixation cross. The duration of decision processes was manipulated by using two stimulus alternatives in half of the blocks (i.e., one color indicated a left response and another color indicated a right response), whereas in the other half of the blocks four stimulus alternatives were used (i.e., two colors indicated a left response and two colors indicated a right response).

Participants are required to make a key press response to a stimulus presented on the left or right side of a fixation cross. Participants were required to respond to a single, lateralized letter (out of a set of four possible letters). For each participant, four consonants (excluding the letter “Z”) were randomly selected for use as stimulus letters, with two each randomly assigned to left and right hand responses. The letter to response mapping was manipulated. For two of the four stimulus letters the S-R mapping was fixed over the whole experiment, whereas for the other two stimulus letters the S-R mapping reversed for each new block. Thus, these two stimuli conditions allow examination of the effects of the strength of the connection of S-R associations (i.e., higher with fixed compared to variable S-R mapping) on the Simon effect with a decision stage manipulation, which rules out the potential processing differences between blocks (e.g., working memory load).
